questions.q: Why is this the board-level item?
questions.a: Because funding and liquidity are forward-looking and structural, not operational. At a loan-to-share near 89%, loans are consuming most of the deposit base, so the funding cushion is thinner than the headline capital ratio suggests. And it is exactly the question an examiner will ask you to defend — which is why the confidence and lineage on each figure matter as much as the figure.

suggested: How is the 89.7% reconciled?
Why are loans growing faster?
What is on-hand liquidity?

questions.a: Total loans divided by total shares: $1.04B over $1.16B. Loan balances come from the core, origination and servicing volume from the lending system, and share balances from the finance and ALM workbook — three sources reconciled into one governed figure rather than three that disagree. 94% confidence, and traceable from core to board brief.

Loan demand has run at about 6.4% year over year — healthy demand, and in itself good news. The problem is the denominator: shares grew only 3.1% over the same period. Growth on the lending side is not the thing to slow; the funding side is the thing to lift.

Two things. The academic calendar drives a predictable summer drawdown as the school year ends, and the newly merged Howard University members are not yet primary depositors — roughly a third of them are. Converting that group is the cheapest share growth available, and it strengthens the funding base directly rather than by buying liquidity.

questions.q: Why not just the funding line?
questions.a: Because it treats the symptom. A standby facility gives immediate certainty and a hard buffer, but it is purchased liquidity at a real cost and it leaves loan-to-share climbing underneath. You would arrive at the same conversation a quarter later, having paid for the delay.

Because it is the only path that both closes the gap now and protects you if the seasonality runs against you. The campaign moves the underlying trend; the line holds the buffer through Q1 if uptake lands at the low edge of the band. Neither alone does both.
